<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{Thm: exist_uniq_power_series}
Let $\bm{x}=\{x_1,\dots,x_d\}$ and $E$ be described as above. Then every $y\in \hat{A}$ can be uniquely written as 
$$
y=\sum_{u\in \mathbb{N}^d} a_ux^u, \quad  a_u\in E ~ {\rm for ~ all ~} u\in \mathbb{N}^d,
$$
where for $u=(u_1,\dots,u_d)\in\mathbb{N}^d$, $x^u=x_1^{u_1} \cdots x_d^{u_d}$.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{Thm: algebraic_eqv_automatic}
With the notation of Theorem \ref{Thm: exist_uniq_power_series}. Assume elements of $\bm{x}$ and $E$ are algebraic over $A$. If $E$ is an $\mathbb{F}_q$-vector subspace of $\hat{A}$, then $y$ is algebraic if and only if $\{a_u\}_{u\in \mathbb{N}^d}$ is $q$-automatic.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- rmk-1: body_md -->
In \Cref{Thm: algebraic_eqv_automatic}, the condition ``$E$ is an $\mathbb{F}_q$-vector subspace of $\hat{A}$" can be equivalently replaced by ``$E$ is an additive subgroup of $\hat{A}$". To see this, one direction is clear. As for the converse statement, first notice that every additive subgroup of $A$ is automatically an $\mathbb{F}_p$-vector subspace, and then use the well-known fact that every $p$-automatic sequence is also a $q$-automatic sequence, see for example \cite{AS-auto-seqn}*{Theorem~6.6.4}. Since we employ the tools from commutative algebra in our proof, the above additive group restriction on $E$ is considered natural.
<!-- end rmk-1 -->
<!-- defn-1: body_md -->
\label{Defn: reg_seq}
Let $M$ be an $A$-module. A sequence of elements $\{x_1,\dots, x_n\}$ of $A$ is said to be {\it $M$-regular} if 
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] $M/(x_1,\dots,x_n)M\neq 0$; 
    \item[(ii)] for each $1\le i\le n$, $x_i$ is not a zero-divisor of $M/(x_1,\dots,x_{i-1})M$.  
\end{itemize}
When $M=A$, an $A$-regular sequence would simply be called a regular sequence. Moreover, if every element $x_i$ is contained in an ideal $\mathfrak{a}$, we say $\{x_1, \dots, x_n\}$ is an ($M$-)regular sequence in $\mathfrak{a}$.
<!-- end defn-1 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{Lem: properties_on_reg_seq} 
Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring, and $\mathfrak{a}$ an ideal of $A$. The following are true: 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The depth of $\mathfrak{a}$ is less than or equal to its height;
    \item $\mathfrak{a}$ shares the same depth with its radical;
    \item Given an $A$-regular sequence $\bm{x}$, and a flat homomorphism $\varphi: A\rightarrow B$. Let $\mathfrak{b}$ be the ideal generated by elements of $\varphi(\bm{x})$.  If $\mathfrak{b}\neq B$, then $\varphi(\bm{x})$ is a $B$-regular sequence. 
    \item $\operatorname{depth}(\mathfrak{a}, A)=\inf\limits_{\mathfrak{p} \supset \mathfrak{a} } \{\operatorname{depth}(\mathfrak{p} A_{\mathfrak{p}}, A_{\mathfrak{p}})\}$, where $\mathfrak{p}$ runs through all prime ideals in $A$ containing $\mathfrak{a}$.  
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
(1) See \cite{Eisenbud}*{Proposition 18.2}. (2) See \cite{Eisenbud}*{Corollary 17.8}. (3) Take $R=M=A$, $S=N=B$ in \cite{Cohen-Macaulay-rings}*{Proposition 1.2}. (4) See \cite{Matsumura-commutative-alg}*{(15.F), Proposition}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- defn-2: body_md -->
\label{Defn: Cohen-Macaulay}
    Let $(A, \mathfrak{m})$ be a Noetherian local ring, then it is called \emph{Cohen-Macaulay} if $\operatorname{depth} \mathfrak{m}=\dim A$. A general Noetherian ring $A$ is \emph{Cohen-Macaulay} if for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$, the corresponding localization $A_\mathfrak{m}$ is Cohen-Macaulay.
<!-- end defn-2 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{Prop: CM_basic_prop}
    Let $(A, \mathfrak{m})$ be a local Noetherian ring. 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item If $A$ is regular, then it is Cohen-Macaulay. 
        \item If $A$ is regular, then any localization of $A$ at a prime ideal is also Cohen-Macaulay. 
        \item If $A$ is Cohen-Macaulay, then a set of elements $\{x_1, \dots, x_r\}$ is a regular sequence if and only if $\dim A/(x_1, \dots, x_r)=\dim A-r$. 
        \item If $A$ is Cohen-Macaulay, and $\{x_1, \dots, x_r\}$ is a regular sequence, then $A/(x_1, \dots, x_r)$ is also Cohen-Macaulay. 
        \item Let $\hat{A}$ be $\mathfrak{m}$-adic completion of $A$. Then $A$ is Cohen-Macaulay if and only if $\hat{A}$ is Cohen-Macaulay.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
For (1)-(4), see for example \cite{Hartshorne}*{II, Theorem~8.21A}, or \cite{Matsumura-commutative-alg}*{(1). p. 121; (2) p.104; (3) p.105; (4) p. 104}. For (5), see \cite{Eisenbud}*{Proposition~18.8}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\cite{Cohen-Macaulay-rings}*{ Theorem~1.1.8}\label{Prop: M_seq_isom_graded_mod}
Let $A$ be a ring, $M$ an $A$-module, $\bm{x}=\{x_1, \cdots, x_n\}$ an $M$-regular sequence, and $\mathfrak{a}=(\bm{x})=(x_1, \cdots, x_n)$. Then the induced map (\ref{Eqn: poly_ring_to_grad_ring}) is an isomorphism. In particular, if $\bm{x}$ is $A$-regular, then $(A/\mathfrak{a}) [X]$ is isomorphic to $G_{\mathfrak{a}}(A)$.
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- defn-3: body_md -->
Let $\bm{x}=\{x_1,\dots, x_n\}$ be a sequence of elements in $A$. Let $\mathfrak{a}$ be the ideal generated by $\bm{x}$. We say $\bm{x}$ is {\it $M$-quasi-regular} if the induced canonical homomorphism (\ref{Eqn: poly_ring_to_grad_ring}) is an isomorphism.
<!-- end defn-3 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{Lem: quasi-reg_eqv_reg}
Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring, and $\bm{x}=\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}$ a sequence of elements in the Jacobson radical of $A$. 
Then $\bm{x}$ is $A$-regular if and only if $\bm{x}$ is $A$-quasi-regular.
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The implication $A$-regular $\Rightarrow$ $A$-quasi-regular is given by Lemma \ref{Prop: M_seq_isom_graded_mod}; for the converse, see \cite{Matsumura-commutative-ring-theory-1986}*{Theorem 16.3} and the remark below it.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
\label{Lem: exist_power_series} 
Let $A$ be an $\mathfrak{a}$-adically complete ring. Let $\bm{x}$ be a sequence of elements in $\mathfrak{a}$, $I=(\bm{x})$ the ideal generated by $\bm{x}$, and $E\subset A$ a set of representatives of $A/I$. 
Then every element $y\in A$ admits a power series expansion with respect to $\bm{x}$ and $E$.
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
It is enough to show that for all $i\ge 0$, there are $y_i=\sum_{|u|\le i}a_ux^u$ such that $y-y_i\in I^{i+1}$. We do this by induction on $i$. For $i=0$, since $E$ is a set of representatives of $A/I$, there exists $a_0\in E$ such that $y-a_0\in I$. Now for $i>0$, suppose we have found $y_{i-1}$. Since $y-y_{i-1}\in I^{i}$. And since $I^{i}$ is generated by $\{x^u: |u|=i\}$. One finds $y-y_{i-1}=\sum_{|u|=i}b_ux^u$ with $b_u\in {A}$ and $|u|=i+1$. Now choose $a_u \in E$ satisfies $a_u-b_u \in I$, and take $y_i=y_{i-1}+\sum_{|u|=i}a_ux^u$. Direct calculation verifies that $y-y_i\in I^{i+1}$. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{Prop: uniq_expan_eqv_quasi-reg}
With the notations and assumptions in \Cref{Lem: exist_power_series}, the following are equivalent: 

(1) for every $y\in A$, there exists a unique power series expansion of $y$ with respect to $\bm{x}$ and $E$;  

(2) $\bm{x}$ is $A$-quasi-regular. \\
If furthermore $A$ is Noetherian, then (1) and (2) are equivalent to 

(3) $\bm{x}$ is $A$-regular.
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
(1)$\Rightarrow$(2). Suppose every $y\in A$ has a unique power series expansion of $y$ with respect to $\bm{x}$ and $E$. We show $\bm{x}$ is $A$-quasi-regular. To the contrary suppose $\bm{x}$ was not $A$-quasi-regular. Then the map $\varphi: (A/I)[X] \rightarrow G_I(A)$ is an epimorphism but not an isomorphism. Write 
$$(A/I)[X]=\bigoplus_{i=0}^\infty M_i,$$ 
where $M_i$ denotes the degree $i$ homogeneous component of $(A/I)[X]$. Noticing that $\varphi$ is a homogeneous homomorphism of graded rings, $\varphi$ maps $M_i$ onto the homogeneous component $I^i/I^{i+1}$ of $G_I(A)$. Since $\varphi$ is not an isomorphism, there exists an integer $i\ge 0$ such that $\varphi|_{M_i}: M_i\rightarrow I^i/I^{i+1}$ is not an isomorphism. So there exists a nonzero homogeneous polynomial $\sum_{|u|=i}\bar{b}_uX^u \in A/I[X]$ satisfying 
$$\varphi\big(\sum_{|u|=i}\bar{b}_uX^u \big)=\sum_{|u|=i}\bar{b}_u\bar{x}^{u}=0 \in I^i/I^{i+1}.$$ 
For fixed $y\in A$, recalling the inductive procedure in the proof of Lemma \ref{Lem: exist_power_series}, suppose we have found a partial sum  
$$y_{i}=\sum_{|u|\le i} a_ux^u, a_u\in E$$
with $y-y_i\in I^{i+1}$. Meanwhile for each $u$ with $|u|=i$, there exists a $c_u\in E$ such that the reduction of $c_u-a_u$ modulo $I$ equals $\bar{b}_u$. Notice that $c_u\neq a_u$ if $\bar{b}_u\neq 0$. Let 
$$y_i'=\sum_{|u|< i} a_ux^u+\sum_{|u|=i}c_ux^u.$$
Then $y_i\equiv y_i' \mod I^i$. So both $y-y_i$ and $y-y_i'$ are in $I^{i+1}$.  Again by the inductive procedure in the proof of Lemma \ref{Lem: exist_power_series}, we can find power series expansions for both $y-y_i$ and $y-y_{i}'$. Expansions $y-y_i$ and $y-y_i'$ add the partial sums $y_i$ or $y_i'$ respectively give different power series expansions of $y$ with respect to $\bm{x}$ and $E$. This contradicts our uniqueness assumption on power series of $y$. Therefore $\bm{x}$ is $A$-qausi-regular. 

(2)$\Rightarrow$(1). Next assume $\bm{x}$ is $A$-quasi-regular. We show there exists a unique power series expansion of $y$ for all $y\in A$. Given $y\in A$, let $\sum_{u\in\mathbb{N}^d} a_ux^u$ and $\sum_{u\in\mathbb{N}^d}b_ux^u$ be two power series expansions of $y$ with respect to $\bm{x}$ and $E$. We show $a_u-b_u=0$ for all $u\in\mathbb{N}^d$. This will be done by induction on $|u|$. 

If $|u|=0$, then $a_0$ (or $b_0$) is the element of $E$ satisfying $y\equiv a_0 \mod I$ (or $y\equiv b_0 \mod I$). So $a_0=b_0$. Suppose $a_u=b_u$ for all $u$ with $|u|<i$. Then 
$$\sum_{|u|=i}a_ux^u-\sum_{|u|=i}b_ux^u\in I^{i+1}.$$
Let $\psi: A[X] \rightarrow G_I(A)$ be the epimorphism induced by $\bm{x}$. Recall that $\varphi(\alpha X^u)=\bar{\alpha}x^u$ for $\alpha\in A$. We deduce that  
$$\varphi(\sum_{|u|=i}a_uX^u)=\varphi(\sum_{|u|=i}b_uX^u).$$
That is $\sum_{|u|=i}(a_u-b_u)X^u\in \ker \psi$. Since $\bm{x}$ is $A$-quasi-regular, $\ker \psi=I[X]$. Thus $a_u-b_u\in I$ for all $u$ with $|u|=i$. But both $a_u$ and $b_u$ are elements of $E$. Hence $a_u=b_u$. This shows the uniqueness of power series expansions of $y$ with respect to $\bm{x}$ and $E$. (1)$\Leftrightarrow$(2) is proved. 

Further assume $A$ is Noetherian. Since $A$ is $\mathfrak{a}$-adically complete, $\mathfrak{a}$ is contained in the Jacobson radical of $A$. So by Lemma \ref{Lem: quasi-reg_eqv_reg}, (2) $\Leftrightarrow$ (3). This finishes the proof of the lemma.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
\label{Lem: height_quot_decomp}
Then the following are equivalent. 

\begin{itemize}
\item[(1)] $\operatorname{height} \mathfrak{a}=\dim A$; 
\item[(2)] $A/\mathfrak{a}$ is a finite ring; 
\item[(3)] $\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{q}_1\cdots\mathfrak{q}_s$, where $\mathfrak{q}_i$ are primary ideals whose radicals are different maximal ideals.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
(1)$\Leftrightarrow$(2). Since $\dim A=\operatorname{height} \mathfrak{a}+ \dim A/\mathfrak{a}$, one sees that $\operatorname{height} \mathfrak{a}=\dim A$ if and only if $\dim A/\mathfrak{a}=0$. The latter happens exactly when $A/\mathfrak{a}$ is Artinian. This is equivalent to saying $A/\mathfrak{a}$ is finitely generated as an $\mathbb{F}_q$-module, in other words, $A/\mathfrak{a}$ is a finite ring. 

(2)$\Leftrightarrow$(3). Let  $\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{q}_1\cdots\mathfrak{q}_s$ be a primary decomposition of $\mathfrak{a}$ such that the radicals of $\mathfrak{q}_i$ are different prime ideals. Then $\operatorname{height} \mathfrak{a}=\dim A$ if and only if the minimum of heights of radicals of $\mathfrak{q}_i$ is $\dim A$, if and only if all radicals of $\mathfrak{q}_i$ are maximal.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lem-5: body_md -->
\label{Lem: dim_height_depth_in_completion}
Under the assumption $\operatorname{height} \mathfrak{a}=d$, we have 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\dim \hat{A}=\operatorname{height} \hat{\mathfrak{a}}=d$; 
    \item every $A$-regular sequence in $\mathfrak{a}$, seen as a sequence in $\hat{\mathfrak{a}}$, is $\hat{A}$-regular. 
    \item $\operatorname{depth} \mathfrak{a}=d$ if and only if $\operatorname{depth} \hat{\mathfrak{a}}=d$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
(1) Let $\mathfrak{a}=\prod_{i=1}^s \mathfrak{q}_i$ be the primary decomposition of $\mathfrak{a}$ as stated in \Cref{Lem: height_quot_decomp}. Let $\mathfrak{m}_i$ be the radical of $\mathfrak{q}_i$. Let $\hat{A}_i$ be the completion of $A_i$ at $\mathfrak{m}_iA_i$. 
Then 
$$\hat{A}=\varprojlim_{n}A/\mathfrak{a}^n \cong \varprojlim_{i} \prod_{i=1}^s A/\mathfrak{q}_i^n 
\cong \prod_{i=1}^s \varprojlim_{n} A/\mathfrak{q}_i^n \cong \prod_{i=1}^s \varprojlim A/\mathfrak{m}_i^n 
\cong \prod_{i=1}^s \hat{A}_i.$$
Since $\dim A=d$, we have $\dim \hat{A}_i=d$ for all $1\le i\le s$. It follows that $\dim \hat{A}=d$. 

By \Cref{Lem: height_quot_decomp}, $\operatorname{height} \mathfrak{a}=d$ implies that $\hat{A}/\hat{\mathfrak{a}}$ ($\cong A/\mathfrak{a}$) is a finite ring. So all prime ideals containing $\hat{\mathfrak{a}}$ are maximal. Meanwhile all maximal ideals of $\hat{A}$ are of the form $\mathfrak{m}_i\hat{A}$. We have $\operatorname{height} \mathfrak{m}_i\hat{A}=\operatorname{height} \mathfrak{m}_i\hat{A}_i=d$. That is, heights of all maximal ideals of $\hat{A}$ are $d$. Thus $\operatorname{height} \hat{\mathfrak{a}}=d$. 

(2) Note that $\hat{A}$ is a flat $A$-algebra. Then (2) follows from \Cref{Lem: properties_on_reg_seq} (3). 

(3) Obviously (2) implies $\operatorname{depth} \mathfrak{a}\le \operatorname{depth} \hat{\mathfrak{a}}$. This together with $\operatorname{depth} \hat{\mathfrak{a}}\le \operatorname{height} \hat{\mathfrak{a}}=d$ deduce $\operatorname{depth} \mathfrak{a}=d \Rightarrow \operatorname{depth} \hat{\mathfrak{a}}=d$. Conversely, suppose $\operatorname{depth} \hat{\mathfrak{a}}=d$, this is equivalent to say $\hat{A}$ is Cohen-Macaulay. Then $\hat{A}_i$, which coincides with the localization of $\hat{A}$ at $\mathfrak{m}_i \hat{A}$, is also Cohen-Macaulay for any $1\le i\le r$. By \Cref{Prop: CM_basic_prop} (5), $A_i$ are Cohen-Macaulay for all $1\le i\le r$, i.e., $\operatorname{depth} (\mathfrak{m}_i A_i, A_i)=d$. Now $\operatorname{depth} \mathfrak{a}=d$ follows from \Cref{Lem: properties_on_reg_seq} (4).
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lem-6: body_md -->
\label{Lem: max_reg_seq_eqv_fin_quot}
Let $\bm{x}=\{x_1,\dots, x_n\}$ be a $\hat{A}$-regular sequence in $\hat{a}$, and $I=(\bm{x})$ the ideal generated by $\bm{x}$. Then $\hat{A}/I$ is a finite ring if and only if $n=d$.
<!-- end lem-6 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Obviously $n\le \operatorname{depth} \hat{\mathfrak{a}} \le \operatorname{height} \hat{\mathfrak{a}}=d$. Suppose $\hat{A}/I$ is a finite ring. Then every prime ideal containing $I$ is maximal. So by the same arguments in the proof of \Cref{Lem: dim_height_depth_in_completion}, we deduce that $\operatorname{height} I=d$. Meanwhile, $\operatorname{height} I\le n$ by \cite{Atiyah-Macdonald}*{Corollary 11.16}. So $d\le n$. Now we conclude that $n=d$. 

Conversely suppose $n=d$. For an integer $m>0$, $\hat{A}/\hat{\mathfrak{a}}^m\cong A/\mathfrak{a}^m$. By the fact that $\operatorname{height} \mathfrak{a}^m=\operatorname{height} \mathfrak{a}=d$ and \Cref{Lem: height_quot_decomp}, we derive that $A/\mathfrak{a}^m$ is a finite ring. Hence it is reduced to showing that $\hat{\mathfrak{a}}^m\subset (\bm{x})$ for some positive integer $m$. It is easy to see both $I$ and $\hat{\mathfrak{a}}$ are contained in Jacobson radical of $\hat{A}$. In the mean time, every prime ideal containing $I$ or $\hat{\mathfrak{a}}$ is maximal. Hence both radicals of $I$ and $\hat{\mathfrak{a}}$ are $\prod_{i=1}^s \mathfrak{m}_i\hat{A}$. Thus $\hat{\mathfrak{a}}^m\subset (\bm{x})$ for certain $m>0$. This ends the proof of this lemma.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{Thm: exist_uniq_power_series_refined}
Let $\bm{x}=\{x_1,...,x_n\}$ be a sequence of elements in $\hat{\mathfrak{a}}$. Write $I=(\bm{x})$. Let $E$ be a set of representatives of $\hat{A}/I$. Then each $y\in \hat{A}$ admits a power series expansion with respect to $\bm{x}$ and $E$. Furthermore the following three statements are equivalent: 

(1) $E$ is finite and for any $y\in \hat{A}$, there exists a unique power series expansion of $y$ with respect to $\bm{x}$ and $E$; 

(2) $\bm{x}$ is a $\hat{A}$-quasi-regular and $n=d$; 

(3) $\bm{x}$ is $\hat{A}$-regular and $n=d$.
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The existence of power series expansion with respect to $\bm{x}$ and $E$ follows from \Cref{Lem: exist_power_series}. Applying \Cref{Prop: uniq_expan_eqv_quasi-reg} to $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{\mathfrak{a}}$, we derive that for any $y\in \hat{A}$, there exists a unique power series expansion of $y$ with respect to $\bm{x}$ and $E$ if and only if $\bm{x}$ is $\hat{A}$-quasi-regular, if and only if $\bm{x}$ is $\hat{A}$-regular. Then by \Cref{Lem: max_reg_seq_eqv_fin_quot}, (1), (2) and (3) are equivalent.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- rmk-2: body_md -->
\Cref{Thm: exist_uniq_power_series} follows immediately from \Cref{Thm: exist_uniq_power_series_refined} and \Cref{Lem: dim_height_depth_in_completion}. {Actually we see that to ensure the finiteness of $E$ and uniqueness of the expansions in \Cref{Thm: exist_uniq_power_series}, our assumption $\operatorname{depth} \mathfrak{a}=d$ is necessary.}
<!-- end rmk-2 -->
<!-- defn-4: body_md -->
\label{Defn: automatic_sequence}
A $d$-dimensional sequence $\{a_u\}_{u\in \mathbb{N}^d}$ over a finite set $\Delta$ is called {\it $k$-automatic} if it is generated by a $d$-dimensional $k$-DFAO. A $d$-dimensional $k$-automatic sequence can also be characterized by its $k$-kernels.
<!-- end defn-4 -->
<!-- defn-5: body_md -->
Given a sequence $\mathcal{S}=\{a_u\}_{u\in \mathbb{N}^d}$, integers $l\ge 0$ and $0\le v_i<k^l$ ($1\le i\le d$),  for any $u=(u_1,\dots,u_d)\in \mathbb{N}^d$, let 
\begin{equation}\label{k-kernel}
b_u:=b_{(u_1,\dots,u_d)}=a_{(k^l u_1+v_1,\dots,k^l u_d+v_d)}.
\end{equation}
Then $\{b_u\}_{u\in \mathbb{N}^d}$ is a subsequence of $\mathcal{S}$. The {\it $k$-kernel}, denoted by $Ker_k(\mathcal{S})$, of $\mathcal{S}$ is defined to be the collection of subsequences of $\mathcal{S}$ given by (\ref{k-kernel}) for all $l\ge 0$ and $0\le v_i<k^l$.
<!-- end defn-5 -->
<!-- lem-7: body_md -->
\label{Lem: k-kernel}
A sequence $\{a_u\}_{u\in\mathbb{N}^d}$ is $k$-automatic if its $k$-kernel is a finite set.
<!-- end lem-7 -->
<!-- lem-8: body_md -->
\label{Lem: auto_tuples}
The sequence $\mathcal{S}$ of $r$-tuples is $k$-automatic if and only if each $\mathcal{S}_i$ is $k$-automatic. Furthermore the complexity of $\mathcal{S}$ is no more than the product of complexities of all $\mathcal{S}_i$.
<!-- end lem-8 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The first statement is obvious, the second statement follows immediately from 
$$Ker_k(\mathcal{S})\subset Ker_k(\mathcal{S}_1)\times \cdots \times Ker_k(\mathcal{S}_r).$$
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lem-9: body_md -->
\cites{Salon87, Salon89}\label{Lem: Salon's thm}
Let $\{a_u\}_{u\in \mathbb{N}^d}$ be a sequence over $\mathbb{F}_q$. Then $\{a_u\}_{u\in \mathbb{N}^d}$ is $q$-automatic if and only if its generating series $\sum_{u\in\mathbb{N}^d}a_u X^u$ is algebraic over $\mathbb{F}_q(X_1,\dots,X_d)$, where $\mathbb{F}_q(X_1,\dots,X_d)$ stands for the field of rational functions over $\mathbb{F}_q$ with variables $X_1,\dots,X_d$.
<!-- end lem-9 -->
<!-- rmk-3: body_md -->
Traditionally there exist two ways to prove Christol's theorem. One is to use Cartier's operators 
$$\Lambda_v \left( \sum_{u\in\mathbb{N}^d} a_uX^u \right)=\sum_{u\in \mathbb{N}^d} a_{qu+v}^{1/q} X^u$$ 
where $v=(v_1,\dots,v_d)$ with $0\le v_i<q$, and the monoid generated by them. The other relies on a result of Fursternburg on diagonals of rational power series. Both ways demand that the coefficients are in a field. If we consider power series in Theorem \ref{Thm: exist_uniq_power_series}, then both ways seemingly do not work.
<!-- end rmk-3 -->
<!-- defn-6: body_md -->
With the above notations,  an element $y\in \hat{A}$ is called {\it $q$-automatic with respect to $\bm{x}$ and $E$} if the sequence of coefficients $\{a_u\}_{u\in\mathbb{N}^d}$ is a $q$-automatic sequence over $E$. When $\bm{x}$ and $E$ are clear from the contents, we simple call this sequence {\it $q$-automatic}.
<!-- end defn-6 -->
<!-- defn-7: body_md -->
An element $y\in \hat{A}$ is called  {\it algebraic (over $A$)} if there exists a polynomial $P(X)\in A[X]$ such that $P(y)=0$.
<!-- end defn-7 -->
<!-- lem-10: body_md -->
\label{Lem: B_poly_ring}
    The Krull dimension of $B$ is $d$. In particular, $x_1, \dots, x_d$ are algebraically independent over $\mathbb{F}_q$, and $B$ is isomorphic to the polynomial ring of $d$ indeterminates over $\mathbb{F}_q$.
<!-- end lem-10 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Only the first statement requires a proof. Since it is easy to see that the $\dim B$ is less than or equal to $d$, we are reduced to showing $\dim B\geq d$. For this, note that since $\{x_1, \dots, x_d\}$ is a regular sequence of $A$ in $\hat{\mathfrak{a}}$. Take $\hat{\mathfrak{m}}$ to be any maximal ideal containing $\hat{\mathfrak{a}}$, then  $\{x_1, \dots, x_d\}$ is again a regular sequence in the localization $\hat{A}_{\hat{\mathfrak{m}}}$. In fact, according to \Cref{Defn: reg_seq}, we know that $\{x_1, \dots, x_d\}$ is regular if and only if the morphism of $\hat{A}$-module 
    \[
    x_{i+1}: \hat{A}/(x_1,\dots, x_i) \to \hat{A}/(x_1,\dots, x_i) , \quad \bar{a}\mapsto \bar{a}x_{i+1}
    \]
    is injective  for every $i=0, \dots, d-1$ (when $i=0$, we take $x_1: \hat{A}\to \hat{A}$). Recall that $\hat{A}_{\hat{\mathfrak{m}}}$ is a flat $\hat{A}$-module, hence tensoring with $\hat{A}_{\hat{\mathfrak{m}}}$ will preserves the injectivity of the induced map 
    \[
     x_{i+1}: \hat{A}_{\hat{\mathfrak{m}}}/(x_1,\dots, x_i) \to \hat{A}_{\hat{\mathfrak{m}}}/(x_1,\dots, x_i).
    \]
    This tells that $\{x_1, \dots, x_d\}$ is also regular in the local ring $\hat{A}_{\hat{\mathfrak{m}}}$. In particular, it is Cohen-Macaulay for $\dim \hat{A}_{\hat{\mathfrak{m}}}=\dim A=d$ (cf. \Cref{Defn: Cohen-Macaulay}). 
    

    Now consider the natural homomorphism of local rings $B_\mathfrak{b}\to \hat{A}_{\hat{\mathfrak{m}}}$. According to the inequality \cite{Eisenbud}*{Theorem~10.10}
    \[
    d=\dim \hat{A}_{\hat{\mathfrak{m}}}\leq \dim B_\mathfrak{b} + \dim \hat{A}_{\hat{\mathfrak{m}}}/\mathfrak{b} \hat{A}_{\hat{\mathfrak{m}}}
    \]
    it suffices to show $ \dim \hat{A}_{\hat{\mathfrak{m}}}/\mathfrak{b} \hat{A}_{\hat{\mathfrak{m}}}=0$. Notice that  
    $
    \hat{A}_{\hat{\mathfrak{m}}}/\mathfrak{b} \hat{A}_{\hat{\mathfrak{m}}}=\hat{A}_{\hat{\mathfrak{m}}}/(\bm{x})
    $. The regularity of the sequence $\{x_1, \dots, x_d\}$ in $\hat{A}_{\hat{\mathfrak{m}}}$ implies that $\dim \hat{A}_{\hat{\mathfrak{m}}}/(\bm{x})=0$ by \Cref{Prop: CM_basic_prop}(3). Hence the desired equality $\dim B=\dim B_\mathfrak{b}=d$ follows.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lem-11: body_md -->
\label{Lem: free_mod}
Assume $E$ is an $\mathbb{F}_q$-vector space. Let $e_1,\dots,e_r$ be an $\mathbb{F}_q$-basis of $E$. Then $$\hat{A}=\hat{B}e_1\oplus \cdots \oplus \hat{B}e_r$$
as $\hat{B}$-modules. In particular, $\hat{A}$ is a free $\hat{B}$-module of rank $r=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q} \hat{A}/(\bm{x})$.
<!-- end lem-11 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
For any $y\in \hat{A}$, by Theorem \ref{Thm: exist_uniq_power_series}, there exists a unique expansion 
$$ y=\sum_{u \in \mathbb{N}^d}a_ux^u$$
with $a_u\in E$. Write $a_u$ as $a_u=a_u^{(1)}e_1+\cdots +a_u^{(r)}{e_r}$ with $a_u^{(i)}\in \mathbb{F}_q$. Then 
$$y=\sum_{u\in \mathbb{N}^d} \sum_{i=1}^r a_u^{(i)}e_i x^u=\sum_{i=1}^r \sum_{u\in \mathbb{N}^d}a_u^{(i)}x^u.$$
Set $y^{(i)}:=\sum_{u\in \mathbb{N}^d}a_u^{(i)}x^u\in \mathbb{F}_q[[x_1,\dots,x_d]]=\hat{B}$. Then for every $y\in \hat{A}$, there exist unique $y^{(1)},\dots,y^{(r)}\in\mathbb{F}_q[[x_1,\dots,x_d]]$ such that $y=y^{(1)}e_1+\cdots y^{(r)}e_r$. Hence we have  $\hat{A}=\hat{B}e_1\oplus \cdots \oplus \hat{B}e_r$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lem-12: body_md -->
\label{Lem: auto_seq_eqv_alg_summand}
Let $y\in \hat{A}$ and $y=y^{(1)}e_1+\cdots y^{(r)}e_r$ with $y^{(i)}\in \hat{B}$. Then 
$y$ is $q$-automatic if and only if each $y^{(i)}$ ($1\le i\le r$) is algebraic.
<!-- end lem-12 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Let $\{a_u\}_{u\in \mathbb{N}^d}$ and $\{a_u^{(i)}\}$ be as in the proof of \Cref{Lem: free_mod}. Then by \Cref{Lem: auto_tuples}, $\{a_u\}_{u\in \mathbb{N}^d}$ is $q$-automatic if and only if for all $1\le i\le r$, $\{a_u^{(i)}\}$ are $q$-automatic, if and only if $y^{(i)}$ are algebraic.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
\label{Thm: free_mod_alg_version}
$A^a=B^ae_1\oplus \cdots \oplus B^ae_r$ is a free $B^a$-module of rank $r$.
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
\label{Prop: Henselian_pair}
    Let $(A, \mathfrak{a})$ be a pair, for a polynomial $f\in A[T]$ let $\bar{f}$ denote the corresponding residue polynomial in the quotient ring $(A/\mathfrak{a})[T]$. Then the following are equivalent: 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ is contained in the Jacobson radical of $A$. For any monic polynomial $f\in A[T]$ and a factorization $\bar{f}=g_0h_0$, with $g_0$ and $h_0$ coprime monic polynomials in the quotient ring $(A/\mathfrak{a})[T]$, there exists a factorization $f=gh$ in $A[T]$ with $g,h$ monic and $\bar{g}=g_0$, $\bar{h}=h_0$. 
        \item Given an \'etale ring homomorphism $A\to A'$ and an $A$-algebra map $\sigma: A'\to A/\mathfrak{a}$, there exists an $A$-algebra map $A'\to A$ lifting $\sigma$. 
        \item For any finite $A$-algebra $B$ the map $B\to B/IB$ induces a bijection on idempotents. 
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
See \cite{stacks-project}*{\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09XI}{Lemma 09XI}} or \cite{Raynaud}*{XI, \S2, Proposition~1}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- defn-8: body_md -->
A pair $(A,\mathfrak{a})$ satisfying any one of the equivalent conditions in \Cref{Prop: Henselian_pair} is called a \emph{henselian pair}.
<!-- end defn-8 -->
<!-- defn-9: body_md -->
\label{Defn: henselization_pair}
    Let $(A, \mathfrak{a})$ be a pair, a \emph{henselization} of $(A, \mathfrak{a})$ is a henselian pair $(A^h, \mathfrak{a}^h)$ together with a morphism of pairs $\iota: (A, \mathfrak{a})\to (A^h, \mathfrak{a}^h)$ which satisfies the universal property: 
    
    For every henselian pair $(B, \mathfrak{b})$ and every morphism $v: (A, \mathfrak{a})\to (B, \mathfrak{b})$, $v$ factors uniquely through a morphism $u: (A^h, \mathfrak{a}^h)\to (B, \mathfrak{b})$, i.e., there is a unique morphism of pair $u$ such that the following diagram is commutative 
    \[
    \begin{tikzcd}
        (A, \mathfrak{a}) \arrow[r, "\iota"] \arrow[rd, "v"']& (A^h, \mathfrak{a}^h) \arrow[d, "\exists ! u"]\\
        & (A, \mathfrak{a})
    \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    We will usually denote the henselization of $(A, \mathfrak{a})$ by $(A, \mathfrak{a})^h$, or even by $A^h$ if there is no danger of confusion. It is easy to see that, when exists, the henselization of a pair is unique up to isomorphism.
<!-- end defn-9 -->
<!-- defn-10: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{I}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ be categories. A ($\mathcal{I}$-)\emph{diagram} in $\mathcal{C}$ is a functor $M: \mathcal{I} \to \mathcal{C}$. We call \emph{index category} of $M$. For each object $i\in \mathcal{I}$, denote by $M_i$ the object in $\mathcal{C}$ corresponding to $i$. The \emph{colimit} of the $\mathcal{I}$-diagram $M$ in $\mathcal{C}$ is an object $\operatorname{colim}_{\mathcal{I}} M$ (or simply $\operatorname{colim} M$) of $\mathcal{C}$ together with morphisms $s_i: M_i \to \operatorname{colim} M$ indexed by objects $i$ in $\mathcal{I}$ such that 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item for $\phi: i \to i'$ a morphism in $I$, we have $s_i =s_{i'} \circ M(\phi)$; 
    \item for any object $W$ in $\mathcal{C}$ and any family of morphisms $t_i: M_i \to W$ indexed by $i\in Ob(\mathcal{I})$ such that for all $\phi: i \to i'$ in $\mathcal{I}$ we have $t_{i}=t_{i'} \circ M(\phi)$, there exists a unique morphism $t: \operatorname{colim} M \to W$ such that $t_i=t \circ s_i$ for every object $i$ of $\mathcal{I}$.   
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end defn-10 -->
<!-- defn-11: body_md -->
A pair over $(R, I)$ is a pair $(S, J)$ together with a morphism $\varphi: (R, I) \to (S, J)$. A pair $(S, J)$ over $(R, I)$ is called an \emph{\'etale neighborhood} of $(R, I)$ if $S$ is an \'etale $R$-algebra, $J=IS$, and the induced residue ring map $R/I \to S/J$ is isomorphic.
<!-- end defn-11 -->
<!-- lem-13: body_md -->
\label{Lem: henselization_local}
    Fixing a pair $(R, I)$, let $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ be as above. 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The category $\mathcal{D}$ is directed. 
        \item $R^h=\operatorname{colim} F$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-13 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
See \cite{stacks-project}*{\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A02}{Lemma 0A02}} and its proof.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lem-14: body_md -->
\label{Lem: henselization_of_etale_neighborhood}
Let $(R, I)$, $(R', I')$ be as the above, and let $\mathcal{D}$ and $\mathcal{D}'$ be the associated categories. The inclusion functor $G$ is a final functor (See \cite{MacLane} for definition of final functors). Hence 
$$(R')^h:=\operatorname{colim} (F \circ G) = \operatorname{colim} F=:R^h.$$
<!-- end lem-14 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
The isomorphism in the middle of the equation is an immediate consequence if $G$ is a final functor. Hence the proof is reduced to checking that $G$ is final. For this, we will need to show the following: 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item for each object $(S, J)$ of $\mathcal{D}$, there exists an object $(S',J')$ of $\mathcal{D}'$ and a morphism $(S, J)\to G(S', J')=(S', J')$ in $\mathcal{D}$.
    \item for any two such morphisms, say $\phi': (S, J)\to (S', j')$ and $\phi'': (S, J)\to (S'', j'')$, there exist finitely many objects $\{(S'_i, J'_i)\}_{i=0, \dots, n}$ such that 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $n$ is even, $(S_0', j'_0)=(S', J')$, $(S'',J'')=(S'_n, J'_n)$;
        \item for each even integer $m\in \{1, \dots, n\}$, there are two morphisms $f_{m-1}, (S_m', J_m')\to (S_{m-1}', J_{m-1}')$ and $f_{m}: (S_m', J_m')\to (S_{m+1}', J_{m+1}')$
        \item for each $i$, a morphism $\phi_i: (S, J)\to G(S_i', J_i')=(S_i', J_i')$; moreover, $\phi_1=\phi'$, $\phi_n=\phi''$
    \end{enumerate}
    and the above objects together with the morphisms fit into a commutative diagram as follow 
    \[
    \begin{tikzcd}
        &&&(S, J)\arrow[dlll, "\phi_0=\phi'"']\arrow[dll, "\phi_1"']\arrow[dl, "\phi_2"']\arrow[rd, "\phi_{2k}"]\arrow[drrr, "\phi_n"]&&&\\
        (S'_0, J'_0) \arrow[r, "f_0"']& (S_1', J_1') & (S_2', J_2')\arrow[l, "f_1"] \arrow[r, "f_2"']& \cdots & (S_{2k}', J_{2k}') \arrow[l, "f_{2k-1}"] \arrow[r, "f_{2k}"']& \cdots & (S_n', J_n')\arrow[l, "f_{n-1}"]
    \end{tikzcd}
    \]
\end{enumerate}
For (1), take any object $(S,J)$ of $\mathcal{D}$, let $S'=S \otimes_R R'$ and $J'=I'(S \otimes_R R')$. Then by basic property of \'etale morphism is stable under tensor product, we know that $S'$ is \'etale over $R'$. Also notice that $S'/J'=(S\otimes_R R')/(S\otimes_R I')=S\otimes_R R'/I'=S/J$. Hence $(S', J')$ is an object of $\mathcal{D}'$. Moreover, the tensor construction of $(S', J')$ induces a morphism $(S, J) \to (S' J')=G(S', J')$. 

As for (2), suppose  $\phi': (S, I) \to (S', J')$ and $\phi'': (S, I) \to (S'', J'')$ to be two morphisms in $\mathcal{D}$, where $(S', J')$ and $(S'', J'')$ are objects of $\mathcal{D}'$. Consider the tensor product $S'\otimes_{S \otimes_R R'} S''$. We claim that $S'\otimes_{S \otimes_R R'} S''$ is \'etale over $R'$. Indeed, in the commutative diagram 
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
    & & S'\arrow[rd, "g'"] & \\
    R' \arrow[r, "\operatorname{id}\otimes \iota"]  & R'\otimes_R S \arrow[rd, "g\otimes \phi''"'] \arrow[ru, "f \otimes \phi'"]  & & S'\otimes_{S \otimes_R R'} S''\\
    & & S'' \arrow[ru, "f'"']&
\end{tikzcd}
\]
every homomorphism is \'etale. Here $\iota: R\to S$, $f: R'\to S'$ and $g: R'\to S''$ are the natural homomorphisms give rise the \'etale structures. And  $f\otimes \phi': R'\otimes_R S\to S'$ and $g\otimes \phi'': R'\otimes_R S\to S''$ are naturally induced homomorphisms. Since both $R'\otimes_R S$ and $S'$ are all \'etale over $R'$, and since $f\otimes \phi'$ is a homomorphism $R'$-algebras, thus it is \'etale by the standard property of \'etale maps (see \cite{stacks-project}*{\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00U7}{Lemma 00U7}}). By the same argument $g\otimes \phi''$ is also \'etale. Then as the homomorphisms induced by tensor product, $f'$ and $g'$ are also \'etale. This verifies our claim. 

Now consider the pair $(S_1', J_1'):=(S'\otimes_{S \otimes_R R'} S'', I'(S'\otimes_{S \otimes_R R'} S''))$, note that 
\[
S'\otimes_{S \otimes_R R'} S''/I'(S'\otimes_{S \otimes_R R'} S'')=S'/I'S'\otimes_{S\otimes_R R'} S''= (S\otimes_R R')/I(S\otimes R')\otimes_{S\otimes_R R'} S''=S''/I''=R'/I'. 
\]
This tells that $(S_1', J_1')$ is an \'etale neighborhood of $(R', I')$, hence an object in $\mathcal{D}'$. 


We take $n=2$, and denote $(S_i', J_i')$ $(i=0,1,2)$ as (a). Consider the next diagram 
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
(S, J) \arrow[r, equal] \arrow[d, "\phi'"] & (S, J) \arrow[d, "\phi_1"] & (S, J) \arrow[l, equal] \arrow[d, "\phi''"] \\
(S', J') \arrow[r, "g'"]  & (S'\otimes_{S \otimes_R R'} S'', I'(S' \otimes_{S \otimes_R R'} S'')) 
& (S'', J'') \arrow[l, "f'"'] 
\end{tikzcd} 
\]
where the homomorphism $\phi_1$ is the composite of $S\to R'\otimes_R S\overset{f}{\to}S' \overset{g'}{\to}S'\otimes_{S \otimes_R R'} S''$. Thus the  commutativity of this diagram follows from that of the previous diagram. Hence this commutative diagram matches the requirements of (b) and (c) of (2). As an immediate consequence, $G: \mathcal{D}' \to \mathcal{D}$ is a final functor, and this ends the proof of the lemma.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lem-15: body_md -->
\label{Lem: completion_henselization_flat_I}
Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring, let $\mathfrak{a}$ be an ideal of $A$. Let $(A^h, \mathfrak{a}^h)$ and $(\hat{A}, \hat{\mathfrak{a}})$ be the associated henselization and completion respectively. 
Then: 
  \begin{enumerate} 
    \item $\mathfrak{a}^h=\mathfrak{a} A^h$, $A/\mathfrak{a}^i\cong A^h/\mathfrak{a}^iA^h$ for any $i>0$; 
    \item $\widehat{A^h}\cong \hat{A}$, where $\widehat{A^h}$ is the $\mathfrak{a}^h$-adic completion of $A^h$; 
    \item $A^h$ is flat over $A$, $\hat{A}$ is faithfully flat over $A^h$; 
    \item if $\mathfrak{a}$ is contained in the Jacobson radical of $A$, then both $A^h$ and $\hat{A}$ are faithfully flat over $A$.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-15 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
See \cite{stacks-project}*{\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0AGU}{Lemma 0AGU}} for (1), \cite{stacks-project}*{\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0AGV}{Lemma 0AGV}} for 
    (2), (3), and \cite{Greco}*{Theorem~6.5} for (4).
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label{Prop: A^h=A^a}
Let $A$ be a finitely generated integral domain over a field, $\mathfrak{a}$ an ideal of $A$ satisfying $\operatorname{depth} \mathfrak{a}=\dim A=d$. Let $(A^h, \mathfrak{a}^h)$ and $(\hat{A},\hat{\mathfrak{a}})$ be henselization and completion of $(A,\mathfrak{a})$ respectively, and let $A^a$ be the algebraic closure of $A$ in $\hat{A}$. Then $A^h=A^a$.
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
\label{Prop: excellent}
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The class of excellent rings contains fields, Noetherian complete local rings and the integer ring $\mathbb{Z}$.
        \item The class of excellent rings is closed under localization, finitely generated extensions of rings, and passing to quotients. 
        \item Assume $R$ to be an excellent ring, and let $S$ be a finitely generated integral $R$-algebra. Take $S'$ to be the integral closure of $R$ in the fraction field of $S$. Then $S'$ is a finitely generated module of $R$. 
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- lem-16: body_md -->
\cite{Artin-approximation}*{Theorem~(I.10), Artin’s approximation theorem}
    Let $R$ be a field or an excellent discrete valuation ring, and let $(A, \mathfrak{p})$ be a pair such that $A$ is an $R$-algebra of finite type, and $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime ideal of $A$. Take $(A^h, \mathfrak{p}^h)$ and $(\hat{A}, \hat{\mathfrak{p}})$ to be the henselization and completion respectively. Given an arbitrary system of polynomial equations 
    \begin{equation}
        f(T)=0, \quad T=(T_1, \dots, , T_N)
    \end{equation}
    with coefficients in $A^h$, a solution $\hat{t}=(\hat{t}_1, \dots, \hat{t}_N)$ with $\hat{t}_i\in \hat{A}$, and an integer $c$, there exists a solution $t=(t_1, \dots, t_N)$ with $t_i\in A^h$ with 
    \[
    t_i\equiv \hat{t}_i \ (\bmod\ \mathfrak{p}^c) \text{ for all }i. 
    \]
<!-- end lem-16 -->
<!-- prop-7: body_md -->
\label{Prop: algebraic_closure}
Take $(A^h, \mathfrak{m}^h)$ and $(\hat{A}, \hat{\mathfrak{m}})$ to be the henselization and completion of $(A, \mathfrak{m})$ respectively. Assume that $A$ is a normal integral domain, then  $A^h$ is the algebraic closure of $A$ in $\hat{A}$.
<!-- end prop-7 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
First, according to the construction of $A$, we know it is excellent and normal, hence $\hat{A}$ is a domain.  Notice that if $B$ is an \'etale $A$ algebra, then $B$ is finite $A$-module. Thus every element $b\in B$ is algebraic over $A$. Hence $A^h$ is  algebraic over $A$ by \Cref{Lem: henselization_local}(2).  
    
    To show $A^h$ is the algebraic closure of $A$ in $\hat{A}$, we still need to show that $A^h$ is algebraically closed inside $\hat{A}$. Assume $\hat{y}\in \hat{A}$ to be an element which satisfies the polynomial equation
    \[
    f(\hat{y})=0, \quad f(t)\in A^h[t].
    \] 
    By Artin's approximation theorem above, for every positive integer $c$, there exists an element $y^h_c\in A^h$ satisfying  
    \begin{equation}\label{Eqn: Artin_approx}
        f(y^h_c)=0, \quad y^h_c\equiv \hat{y}\ \bmod\ (\mathfrak{m}^h)^c.
    \end{equation}
    By the fundamental theorem of algebra we know that $f(t)$ has at most $\deg(f)$ many roots in $\hat{A}$ or its fraction field. Hence as $c$ increases (for example, when $c\gg 0$ so that $|(\mathfrak{m}^h)^c|$ is smaller than the distance of any two distinct roots of $f(t)$), \eqref{Eqn: Artin_approx} tells that $\hat{y}=y^h_c$ is inside $A^h$. Hence every polynomial over $A^h$ has a root inside $A^h$, i.e., $A^h$ is algebraically closed in $\hat{A}$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lem-17: body_md -->
\label{Lem: henselization_radical_intersection}
Let $(R,I)$ be a pair, $(R^h, I^h)$ be the henselization of $(R, I)$. 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item If $(S,J)$ is the henselization of $(R, \sqrt{I})$, then $(R^h,I^h)=(S,IS)$, and $J=\sqrt{IS}$. 
    \item If $I=I_1 \cap \cdots \cap I_n$, where $I_1,\dots, I_n$ are ideals of $R$ such that $I_i+I_j=R$ for all $1\le i<j\le n$, then the canonical map 
    $$(R,I)^h \to \prod_{i=1}^n (R,I_i)^h$$
    is an isomorphism. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-17 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
(1) See \cite{Greco}*{Proposition 8.6}. (2) See \cite{stacks-project}*{\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0H7Q}{Lemma 0H7Q}}.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lem-18: body_md -->
Under the above setups, $C^h$ is the algebraic closure of $C$ in $\hat{C}$.
<!-- end lem-18 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Since $\mathfrak{m}$ is the maximal ideal of $A$ and $C$ is a finite $A$-algebra, the prime ideals of $C$ containing $mC$ are all maximal. Suppose they are denoted as $\mathfrak{n}_1, \dots, \mathfrak{n}_n$, then the radical $\sqrt{\mathfrak{m} C}$ of $\mathfrak{m} C$ is $\prod_{i=1}^n \mathfrak{n}_i$. For $1\le i\le n$, let $\hat{C}_i$ be the completion of $C$ at $\mathfrak{n}_i$ respectively. It is easy to see that 
$$
\hat{C}\cong \prod_{i=1}^n \hat{C}_i.
$$ 
It then follows from the definition of algebraic closure that $C^a$ is isomorphic to the direct product of the algebraic closures $C^a_i$ of $C$ in $\hat{C}_i$. Since $C$ is normal, $C^a_i=C^h_i$ by \Cref{Prop: algebraic_closure}, where $C^h_i$ is the henselization of $(C, \mathfrak{n}_i)$. On the other hand, by \Cref{Lem: henselization_radical_intersection}(2) we have 
$$C^h \cong \prod_{i=1}^k C_i^h.$$ 
Hence the lemma follows from the equality
$$C^a=\prod_{i=1}^k C^a_i=\prod_{i=1}^k C^h_i=C^h.$$
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lem-19: body_md -->
\label{Lem: completion_henselization_flat}
With $(A, \mathfrak{m})$, $(C, \mathfrak{c})$ and $(C_i, \mathfrak{n}_i)$ as the above, we have 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $C$ is faithfully flat over $A$;
        \item $A^h$ and $\hat{A}$ are faithfully flat over $A$.
        \item $C^h$ and $\hat{C}$ are faithfully flat over $C$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-19 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
By the construction of $C$, it is a finite module of $A$ by \Cref{Prop: excellent}(3), hence is flat over $A$. Moreover, due to the going-up theorem \cite{Atiyah-Macdonald}*{Theorem~5.11} the natural morphism $\operatorname{Spec}(C)\to \operatorname{Spec}(A)$ is surjective. Thus the faithfully flatness follows from the fact that a surjective flat morphism is faithfully flat \cite{MilEC}*{Proposition~2.7}. This proves (1). The rest statements are immediate consequences of \Cref{Lem: completion_henselization_flat_I}(4).
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lem-20: body_md -->
\cite{Atiyah-Macdonald}*{Proposition~10.13}\label{Lem: completion_base_change}
    If $R$ is Noetherian and $M$ is a finitely generated module of $R$, then the above map $\hat{R}\otimes_R M\to \hat{M}$ is isomorphic.
<!-- end lem-20 -->
<!-- lem-21: body_md -->
\cite{stacks-project}*{\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0DYE}{Lemma 0DYE}}\label{Lem: henselization_base_change}
    Let $(R, I)\to (S, J)$ be a map of pairs such that the prime ideals of $S$ containing $IS$ are in bijection with those containing $J$. Let $(R^h, I^h)\to (S^h, J^h)$ be the induced map of henselizations. If $S$ is integral over $R$, then the naturally induced map $R^h\otimes_R S\to S^h$ is an isomorphism.
<!-- end lem-21 -->
<!-- lem-22: body_md -->
\label{Lem: iota_inj}
    The map $\iota$ is injective.
<!-- end lem-22 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
According to \Cref{Lem: completion_base_change} and \Cref{Prop: excellent}(3) we can write $\hat{C}=C^h\otimes_{A^h} \hat{A}$. Under this identity the map 
    \[
        \iota:  C^h \otimes_{A^h} C^h\otimes_{A^h} A^h\cong C^h \otimes_{A^h} C^h \to  (C^h\otimes_{A^h} \hat{A})\otimes_{\hat{A}} (C^h\otimes_{A^h} \hat{A})\cong (C^h\otimes_{A^h} C^h)\otimes_{A^h} \hat{A}
    \]
    is induced by sending elements $(c_1\otimes_{A^h}c_2)\otimes_{A^h} a$ to $c_1\otimes_{A^h}c_2\otimes_{A^h} a$, i.e., $\iota={\rm id}_{C^h\otimes_{A^h} C^h}\otimes {\rm id_{A^h}}$. 
    
    Since $A^h \hookrightarrow \hat{A}$ is injective, the injectivity of $\iota$ is a consequence of the faithfully flatness of $C^h\otimes_{A^h} C^h$ as an $A^h$-module. In the following commutative diagram of rings
    \[
    \begin{tikzcd}
        C^h\otimes_{A^h} C^h & C^h=C\otimes_A A^h \arrow[l] & \arrow[l]C\\
        C^h \arrow[u, "g"]& A^h \arrow[u, "f^h"] \arrow[l, "f^h"']& A \arrow[u, "f"] \arrow[l]
    \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    where $C^h=C\otimes_A A^h$ for \Cref{Lem: henselization_base_change}. The natural inclusion map $f$ is faithfully flat by \Cref{Lem: completion_henselization_flat}(1), hence so are the induced maps $f^h$ and $g$ due to the fact that faithfully flatness is stable under base change \cite{Matsumura-commutative-alg}*{(4.B)}. Hence  the composition $g\circ f^h$ is faithfully flat and our desired property is true.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lem-23: body_md -->
\label{Lem: ff_descent}
    In \eqref{Eqn: 21} the kernel of $d^h$ (resp. $\hat{d}$) is $A^h$ (resp. $\hat{A}$).
<!-- end lem-23 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
By the same arguments in the proof of \Cref{Lem: iota_inj}, one deduces that $C^h$ (resp. $\hat{C}$) is faithfully flat over $A^h$ (resp. $\hat{A}$). Then the desired result follows from the classical descent theory (see \cite{MilEC}*{Proposition~2.18} for instance).
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- prop-8: body_md -->
\label{Prop: algebraic_closure_revisited}
\Cref{Prop: algebraic_closure} is still true without assuming $A$ is normal.
<!-- end prop-8 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
To save notations, we will identify every element of a ring in \eqref{Eqn: 21} with its image via any (composition of) maps in this diagram. To prove this result, we need to show that for every nonzero polynomial $f(T)\in A^h[T]$, each root $a$ in $\hat{A}$ is also contained in $A^h$. But this follows from a diagram chase of \eqref{Eqn: 21} and \Cref{Lem: iota_inj} and \Cref{Lem: ff_descent}. To be more precise, we consider $f(T)$ as a polynomial in $C^h[T]$. Let $a$ be a $\hat{C}$-solution of $f(T)$, then by \Cref{Prop: algebraic_closure}, $a$ is automatically in $C^h$. Since $a\in \hat{A}$ by our assumption, we have $\hat{d}(a)=0$ according to \Cref{Lem: ff_descent}. Using the injectivity of $\iota$ (by \Cref{Lem: iota_inj}) and the commutativity of the diagram, it follows that $d^h(a)=0$ as well. But by \Cref{Lem: ff_descent} again this tells $a\in A^h$. This finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
Let $\mathfrak{a}=\prod_{i=1}^s \mathfrak{q}_i$ be the primary decomposition of $\mathfrak{a}$. For any $1\le i\le s$, let $\mathfrak{m}_i$ be the radical of $\mathfrak{q}_i$. Then $\mathfrak{m}_1, \dots, \mathfrak{m}_s$ are all the maximal ideals of $A$ containing $\mathfrak{a}$, and $\sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}=\mathfrak{m}_1 \cdots \mathfrak{m}_s$. Let $A_i$ be the localization of $A$ at $\mathfrak{m}_i$, and $A_i^h=(A_i, \mathfrak{m}_iA_i)^h$. Then by \Cref{Lem: henselization_radical_intersection}, 
$$A^h=(A, \sqrt{\mathfrak{a}})^h \cong \prod_{i=1}^s (A, \mathfrak{m}_i)^h \cong \prod_{i=1}^s A_i^h.$$  
Meanwhile $\prod_{i=1}^s A^a_i \cong A^a$. Since each $A_i$ is local, \Cref{Prop: algebraic_closure_revisited} implies that $A^h_i=A^a_i$. Hence we conclude that $A^h=A^a$.  \hfill$\Box$
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- defn-12: body_md -->
\cite{stacks-project}*{\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00PL}{Definition 00PL}}\label{Defn: quasi_finite}
Let $R \to S$ be a  homomorphism of rings. Let $\mathfrak{q}$ be a prime ideal of $S$ and let  $\mathfrak{p}=R\cap \mathfrak{q}$ be a prime ideal of $R$. Denote by $\kappa(\mathfrak{q})$ (resp. $\kappa(\mathfrak{p})$) the fraction field of $S/\mathfrak{q}$ (resp. $R/\mathfrak{p}$). We say the ring map $R \to S$ is {\it quasi-finite} at $\mathfrak{q}$ if $S_{\mathfrak{q}}/\mathfrak{p} S_{\mathfrak{q}}$ is of dimension zero and $\kappa(\mathfrak{q})/\kappa(\mathfrak{p})$ is a finite field extension.
<!-- end defn-12 -->
<!-- lem-24: body_md -->
\cite{stacks-project}*{\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/05WP}{Lemma 05WP}}\label{Lem: henselization_and_quasi-finite}
With the notations in \Cref{Defn: quasi_finite}, the homomorphism $R \to S$ induces a commutative diagram 
\[\begin{tikzcd}
   R \arrow[d] \arrow[r] & R_{\mathfrak{p}} \arrow[d] \arrow[r] &  R_{\mathfrak{p}}^h \arrow[d] \\ 
   S           \arrow[r] & S_{\mathfrak{q}}           \arrow[r] &  S_{\mathfrak{q}}^h 
\end{tikzcd}
\]
where $R_{\mathfrak{p}}^h$ and $S_{\mathfrak{q}}^h$ denote henselizations (at their maximal ideals) of local rings $R_{\mathfrak{p}}$ and $S_{\mathfrak{q}}$ respectively. Assume $R \to S$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak{q}$. Then the ring map $R_{\mathfrak{p}}^h \to S_{\mathfrak{q}}^h$ is finite.
<!-- end lem-24 -->
<!-- lem-25: body_md -->
\label{Lem: $A^h$_fin_over_$B^h$}
$A^h$ is a finite $B^h$-module.
<!-- end lem-25 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
As explained above \Cref{Defn: quasi_finite}, it is sufficient to show that, for each $i$, $(A_i')^h$ is finite over $B^h$. By \Cref{Lem: henselization_and_quasi-finite}, this is reduced to showing that the ring homomorphism $B \to A'$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak{m}_i$ for every $i$. 

By construction, we have $\dim A/\mathfrak{a}=0$. Since $A'/\mathfrak{b} A'\cong (A/\mathfrak{b} A)\otimes_{A} A'$. Note that $A'$ is \'etale over $A$, hence $(A/\mathfrak{b} A)\otimes_{A} A'$ is \'etale over $A/\mathfrak{b} A$ by base change. In particular $\dim A'/\mathfrak{b} A'=\dim A/\mathfrak{b} A=0$. On the other hand, $A'/\mathfrak{m}_i$ is clearly finite over $\mathbb{F}_q=B/\mathfrak{b}$. Hence we conclude that the ring map $B\to A'$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak{m}_i$. It follows that $(A_i')^h$ is finite over $B^h$ and proves the lemma.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
By \Cref{Prop: A^h=A^a}, $A^a=A^h$, hence it is equivalent to show that $A^h$ is a free $B^h$-module of rank $r=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q} \hat{A}/(\bm{x})$. Choose $e_1, \dots, e_r\in A^h\subset \hat{A}$ such that their reductions $\bar{e}_1, \dots, \bar{e}_r$ modulo $(\bm{x})$ form an $\mathbb{F}_q$-basis of $\hat{A}/(\bm{x})$. Then $\{\bar{e}_1, \dots, \bar{e}_r\}$ is also an $\mathbb{F}_q$-basis of $A^h/\mathfrak{b} A^h$. By \Cref{Lem: $A^h$_fin_over_$B^h$} we know that $A^h$ is a finite $B^h$-module, then Nakayama's Lemma tells that $\{e_1, \dots, e_r\}$ generates $A^h$ as a $B^h$-module. But \Cref{Lem: free_mod} tells us that $e_1, \dots, e_r$ are also a $\hat{B}$-basis of $\hat{A}$, hence are independent over $B^h$. We then derive that $e_1, \dots, e_r$ consist of a $B^h$-basis of $A^h$. Thus $A^h$ is a free $B^h$-module of rank $r$. This concludes the proof of \Cref{Thm: free_mod_alg_version}. \hfill$\Box$
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- thm-5: body_md -->
\label{Thm: beta expansions}
Let $\beta\in\mathbb{F}_q((1/z))$ be a formal Laurent series of positive degree. Then the following statements are equivalent: 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\beta$ is algebraic;
    \item $d_{\beta}(1)$ is $q$-automatic; 
    \item for any $y\in \mathbb{F}_q[[1/z]]$, $d_{\beta}(y)$ is $q$-automatic if and only if $y$ is algebraic.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-5 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
(2) $\Rightarrow$ (1) is a result of Hbaib and Mkaouar \cite{Hbaib-Mkaouar}. (3) $\Rightarrow$ (2) is obvious. Hence it remains to show (1) $\Rightarrow$ (3). 

Suppose $\beta$ is algebraic. It is easy to see $d_{\beta}(y)$ is $q$-automatic if and only if $d_{\beta}(\beta y-a_1)$ is $q$-automatic. Notice that $\beta y-a_1=\beta y-[\beta y]\in \frac{1}{z}\mathbb{F}_q[[1/z]]$. So it is enough to show (1) $\Rightarrow$ (3) for all $y\in\frac{1}{z}\mathbb{F}_q[[1/z]]$. Now by replacing $y$ with $T(y)$ if necessary,  we can assume $y\in\frac{1}{z}\mathbb{F}_q[[1/z]]$. Suppose $y=\frac{a_1}{\beta}+\frac{a_2}{\beta^2}+\cdots$ to be the $\beta$-expansion of $y$. Write $d\coloneqq \deg \beta$, then 
$$\frac{\beta y}{z^{d-1}}=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{a_i}{z^{d-1}} \frac{1}{\beta^{i-1}}.$$ 
Notice that for any element $y'\in \frac{1}{z}\mathbb{F}_q[[1/z]]$ one has $\deg [\beta y']< \deg \beta$, also notice that the fraction part of any formal Laurent series is contained in $ \frac{1}{z}\mathbb{F}_q[[1/z]]$. Thus one can check that $\deg a_i< \deg \beta$ inductively. So for every $i$, $\frac{a_i}{z^{d-1}}$ is contained in the $\mathbb{F}_q$-subspace 
$\bigoplus_{j=0}^{d-1} \frac{1}{z^j}\mathbb{F}_q.$

Take $A=\mathbb{F}_q[1/z]$. Notice that $\bm{x}=\{\beta\}$ is a regular sequence in the ideal $\mathfrak{a}=\frac{1}{z}\mathbb{F}_q[[1/z]]$. Let $E=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{d-1} \frac{1}{z^j}\mathbb{F}_q$.  Then 
$$\frac{\beta y}{z^{d-1}}=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{a_i}{z^{d-1}} \frac{1}{\beta^{i-1}}$$
is the expansion of $\frac{\beta y}{z^{d-1}}$ with respect to $E$ and $\bm{x}$. Hence $y$ is algebraic if and only if $\frac{\beta y}{z^{d-1}}$ is algebraic, and the latter holds if and only if $\{\frac{a_i}{z^{d-1}}\}_{i\ge 1}$ is $q$-automatic  according to \Cref{Thm: algebraic_eqv_automatic}. Finally, it is obvious that  $\{\frac{a_i}{z^{d-1}}\}_{i\ge 1}$ is $q$-automatic exactly when $d_{\beta}(y)$ is $q$-automatic. This proves (1) $\Rightarrow$ (3) and completes the proof of this theorem.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
